clue.text: Likable general speaking after pressure to confess

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure

indicators.note: speaking means the word is heard rather than read, so its sound counts and its spelling may change

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general; LEA, a meadow, is said the same way
to sing is slang for confessing to the police

explanation.surface: A charming general pressed into making a confession under interrogation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the general's sound behind the pressure; the confession then follows on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pleasing gives enjoyment, so a pleasing person is agreeable and easy to like.

clue.text: Lichtenstein espoused it as an interest outside work

indicators.note: one thing placed outside another wraps around it on both sides

parts.note: a part is a share, an interest in a venture
OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: An artist who took up something as a hobby away from the day job.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy Lichtenstein, the American painter of comic-strip images, was a leading figure in the movement; 'espoused' points to the cause he championed.
explanation.definitionFit: Lichtenstein's comic-book paintings are textbook examples of the 1960s movement drawing on mass culture and advertising.

clue.text: Start with money to maintain Anglesey's principal harbour

parts.note: to enter on something is to start it

indicators.note: to maintain something is to hold and keep it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: tin is old slang for money

indicators.note: the principal part of a word is its leading letter

parts.note: the Welsh island's opening letter

explanation.surface: Raising funds to keep up the main port on Anglesey, the Welsh island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbour' reads as the noun from the island setting, but it is a verb, as in harbouring a doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an idea or hope is to keep it in mind, just as one harbours a suspicion.

clue.text: Schoolboy possibly rejecting award from The Sun

indicators.note: rejecting something means throwing it out, so letters are removed

parts.note: a schoolboy is one example of a pupil, hence 'possibly'
CH is the Companion of Honour, a British award

explanation.surface: A pupil turning down a prize offered by The Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make The Sun a tabloid newspaper, but the definition means our star.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything coming from or relating to the star at the centre of our planetary system.

clue.text: Grandma eager to find a hard-wearing fabric

parts.note: nan is an informal word for grandmother
keen means eager

explanation.surface: A granny keen to track down some tough cloth for sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: A plain two-part build; the knowledge needed is the fabric itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Nankeen is a durable yellowish cotton cloth, originally made in Nanjing, used for trousers and work clothing.

clue.text: Boss at satellite TV production company

parts.note: a stud or boss is a raised knob on a surface
Io is one of Jupiter's moons

explanation.surface: The head of a satellite television firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' wants to be the person in charge; here it is the ornamental knob. 'Satellite' sits naturally with TV but means a moon.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio is a firm that makes films or programmes, named after the premises where they are shot.

clue.text: Kitty turned up with an artist of the highest standing

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something up flips it to read bottom to top

parts.note: the kitty or pot is the pool of stakes in a card game
one who draws is an artist

explanation.surface: A cat appears alongside a celebrated painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' suggests a cat, but it is the gambling pool.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people of the best social class or quality, from the top drawer holding the finest things.

clue.text: Follow most of Chinese revolutionary's code of principles

indicators.note: most of a thing is all but a little, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
Mao Zedong led the Chinese Communist revolution

explanation.surface: Adhering to a Chinese revolutionary leader's set of beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as following Mao's doctrine, which is exactly what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogma is a fixed set of beliefs laid down by an authority and held as unquestionably true.

clue.text: Cast to repeat light-hearted theatrical production

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould, so the letters are thrown into a fresh shape

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Actors hired to reprise a comic stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' reads as the noun for a show's performers, fitting the theatre picture, but it is a verb signalling rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An operetta is a short comic opera with spoken dialogue and a light, romantic story.

clue.text: Native American back in factory showing peevish impatience

indicators.note: something put in another thing sits inside it

parts.note: a plant is an industrial works

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: the Ute are a Native American people of Utah and Colorado

explanation.surface: A Native American, back at work in the factory, looking irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ute tribe gives the classic three-letter crossword Native American.
explanation.definitionFit: Petulant describes someone sulky and bad-tempered like a child who cannot get their way.

clue.text: Culmination of attempt to pursue secretary brought about by drugs

indicators.note: a ship brought about turns to face the opposite way

parts.note: to have a go is to make an attempt
PA is a personal assistant
E is ecstasy, so two doses give drugs in the plural

explanation.surface: Someone's bid to chase a secretary reaches its climax while high on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The attempt is set beside the secretary and the pair is turned round; two Es for ecstasy go on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The apogee is the highest point of an orbit, and figuratively the climax or peak of anything.

clue.text: Second bed tax

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A levy on owning a second bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Britain's controversial 'bedroom tax' on spare rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Scot is an old word for a local levy or payment, surviving in the phrase scot-free.

clue.text: Less widely known rule on poison copper ignored

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it, so the first-named piece is placed second
what is ignored is left out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: curare is a plant poison used on arrow tips
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
R is a dictionary abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: An obscure regulation about poisons, with copper not included.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, so the rule follows the trimmed poison.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rarer is found less often, so fewer people are familiar with it.

clue.text: Strongly criticise erotica produced by former partner

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: something produced has been made or worked up, so these letters are fashioned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Condemning the racy material made by someone's ex.
explanation.walkthrough: The former partner leads, followed by the reworked letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To excoriate literally means to strip the skin, and figuratively to denounce someone savagely.

clue.text: Two bodies of water both short of fish

indicators.note: both short means each of the pair lacks its end, so every word loses its final letter

parts.note: a tarn is a small mountain lake
a pond is a small still body of water

explanation.surface: Two lakes that are both lacking in fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both short' means each of the two waters is docked, not just one.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarpon is a large silvery game fish of warm Atlantic waters, prized by anglers.

clue.text: Managed to replace filter

indicators.note: managed suggests things handled and arranged, so these letters are reorganised

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone succeeded in swapping out a filter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Managed' reads as succeeded, but it signals the rearrangement; 'filter' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To percolate is to pass slowly through a porous material, as water does through coffee grounds.

clue.text: Tug at boot with wife cracking up

indicators.note: something cracking up is breaking apart, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Someone yanks at a boot while his wife falls about laughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tug' looks like a verb pulling at the boot, but it is the noun for a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tug is a small powerful vessel used for pulling or pushing larger ships, also called a towboat.

clue.text: Began to admit part in allowing free expressions of opinion

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: to open is to begin
an end is a part or portion, as in 'your end of the deal'

explanation.surface: Someone started to confess some involvement while letting others speak freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Began to admit' looks like the start of a confession, but 'to admit' is the instruction to insert.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-ended question has no fixed answer, inviting the respondent to give their own views at length.

clue.text: Scratch from game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to scrape or claw about with the hands
second meaning: the board game of making words from lettered tiles

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests withdrawing from a match, as a scratched entrant does.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to grope or claw frantically, and the noun is the trademarked word-building board game.

clue.text: Check company books with Rob endlessly

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
to roll someone is slang for robbing them

explanation.surface: Auditing a firm's accounts alongside a man called Rob, who goes on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rob' looks like a name because of its capital, but it is the verb meaning steal from.
explanation.definitionFit: To check something is to restrain or keep it in hand, which is to control it.

clue.text: Helping to make Bale analogy unproductive

indicators.note: these words only help to make up a word, contributing a portion of their letters

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Gareth Bale, the Welsh footballer, offering a comparison that gets nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital invites the footballer, but the name is only there for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lean years or lean times are periods of scarcity, when little is produced or earned.

clue.text: Bronwen regularly invading my secret place

indicators.note: an invader goes inside a territory, so one piece enters another

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the Welsh name

explanation.surface: Bronwen keeps intruding on a private hideaway of mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive, but it is the exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A corner is a quiet, out-of-the-way spot, as in a hidden corner of the garden.

clue.text: Lower the reputation of revolutionary American writer

parts.note: Che Guevara is crosswords' favourite revolutionary
A is the abbreviation for American
a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: Damaging the good name of a radical American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective for the writer, but it is the guerrilla leader himself.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheapen someone is to degrade them and lessen the respect in which they are held.

clue.text: On bad terms with Dorothy over splitting bills

indicators.note: something splitting another wedges itself into the middle of it

parts.note: ads and bills are both advertisements

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so in a down entry the letters read upward

parts.note: Dot is a short form of Dorothy

explanation.surface: Falling out with Dorothy after arguing over how to divide up the bills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bills' suggests invoices to share, but they are posters.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people at odds are in disagreement or conflict with each other.

clue.text: A random charge on port

indicators.note: random means in no set order, so the letters are scattered afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An arbitrary fee levied on the drink port, or on a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Random' sits in the middle of its fodder, splitting the letters into two runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Anchorage is Alaska's main port city, and the word also means any place where ships anchor.

clue.text: Imprisons Catholic girl heartlessly

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Catholic
a girl's name, as so often in crosswords

explanation.surface: Locking up a Catholic girl without mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessly' reads as cruelly, but it removes the middle letter of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To cage someone is to confine them as though behind bars, which is imprisoning them.

clue.text: Told to go in conversation with guide

indicators.note: in conversation words are heard, not seen, so only the sound matters

parts.note: someone told to go has been dispatched

explanation.surface: Someone being dismissed in the middle of a chat with a guide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guide' looks like a person in the scene, but it is the noun for what leads a hound along a trail.
explanation.definitionFit: A scent is the trail of smell left by an animal, which hounds follow, so it acts as their guide.

clue.text: Difficult actress runs away

indicators.note: what goes away is no longer there, so letters are taken out

parts.note: Meryl Streep, the American actress
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A temperamental actress walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs away' looks like the actress fleeing, but 'runs' is a letter to remove and 'away' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep demand or climb is hard to meet or manage, so it is difficult.

clue.text: Exhaust horse during show

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: to bear is to show, as in bearing a scar
gee-gee is a childish word for a horse

explanation.surface: Wearing out a horse during a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' suggests a horse show, but it is the verb meaning display.
explanation.definitionFit: To beggar something, as in 'beggars belief', is to exhaust its resources or go beyond its capacity.

clue.text: Brilliant odds against Close wearing a hat

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the betting odds at the start of a race

indicators.note: what is worn sits around its wearer, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: lid is slang for a hat
the close of something is its end

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's bet against Glenn Close, the actress, appearing in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Close' suggests the actress; it is just the noun for an ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendid and brilliant both mean excellent or magnificent, used as words of high praise.

clue.text: Not as strict when that's accepted by Her Maj

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so it ends up inside the other piece

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the late Queen's cipher
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
i.e. stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: The Queen is more relaxed when something is approved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her Maj' is British slang for Her Majesty the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Easier rules or teachers are more lenient, demanding less, which is to say less strict.

clue.text: Extremely stylish suit

parts.note: in means fashionable
spades is one of the four suits in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A very fashionable set of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' suggests clothing to go with 'stylish', but it is a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in large amounts or to a great degree, so it works as an intensifier.
